CHAPTER ONE

The alarm's shrill beep pierced through Claudia Murphy's dream. She would have liked to stay in it longer, but the morning light streaming through her bedroom window pulled her into wakefulness. The dream faded. Claudia threw off her blanket, swung her feet to the floor, and reached for her tablet on the nightstand.

She heard her mother's quick footsteps in the hallway. They paused outside her bedroom door.

"You awake, Claudia?"

"I'm awake, Mom," Claudia answered.

"Breakfast is ready. Get dressed and come eat."

"Be right there," Claudia said. Then, remembering the dream, she added, "Oh, Mom, is it all right if I use the spectral analyzer today?"

Dr. Margaret Kim opened the door. She was a tall woman, athletic and energetic despite her demanding schedule. Claudia found it easy to believe the stories about her mother being a champion swimmer in college. Even her reading glasses and the gray streaks in her black hair didn't add much age, although Claudia knew it had been twenty years since her mother had competed in her last collegiate meet.

"You may use the spectral analyzer any time you want, Claudia," Dr. Kim said, "as long as you handle it carefully. You figured out where you might find contaminated samples?"

Claudia smiled sheepishly. "I—I had a dream," she said. "Clear as anything. It was out at the old industrial site near Timberline. I was scanning some soil samples. Suddenly the analyzer started showing elevated readings of heavy metals."

"The Timberline site?" her mother asked. "I've never been out there myself. But from what I hear, there's plenty of ground that was never properly remediated after the factories closed. Might be worth investigating. You never know what environmental hazards might still be lurking there."

"Do you believe in dreams, Mom?"

"Well, that's a complicated question, dear. I can't say that I really do. Still, one hypothesis is as good as another when it comes to environmental health research, I suppose. But right now we'd better get to breakfast before your father leaves for work. Hurry up." Her mother turned and headed back toward the kitchen.

Claudia pulled on her jeans and a clean shirt and went into the bathroom. She washed quickly, knowing that even if she missed a spot or two, she was fairly safe during summer break. She ran a brush through her shoulder-length brown hair and examined her reflection. The braces on her teeth caught the light.

She carefully removed the small rubber bands from her braces and dropped them in the waste basket. She'd put fresh ones in after breakfast.

She brushed her teeth meticulously, taking special care around the metal brackets. The orthodontist had warned her about letting food particles accumulate around the braces. It could lead to cavities.

Finished, Claudia went out to breakfast.

"Good morning, sweetheart," her father greeted her, pouring orange juice into her glass.

"Hi, Dad," Claudia said. "Big plans today."

"So your mother tells me. But I'm afraid your big plans will have to start with organizing the recycling bins in the garage," her father said.

"Aw, Dad—"

"Claudia, I asked you to do it four days ago. Remember? And the municipal pickup is this afternoon."

"But, Dad—"

"No arguments, dear," her mother said firmly but kindly. "Summer vacation doesn't mean your responsibilities around here are on vacation too. Get it done right away, and you'll still have time for your environmental survey."

"Well," Mr. Kim added, excusing himself from the table, "I'd better head out. We're expecting a major shipment today—it's leaving the pharmaceutical research facility in Lincoln early this morning and should arrive by mid-afternoon. Timing is critical with temperature-sensitive cargo."

The very mention excited Claudia. In fact, anything having to do with public health and supply chain management excited her. She knew something about pharmaceutical distribution—you couldn't have a father who was operations manager without picking up knowledge along the way. Claudia knew that proper supply chain management was critical for getting medications to clinics and hospitals on time, especially for temperature-sensitive vaccines and biologics.

"Where exactly is the shipment coming from in Lincoln?" Claudia asked, then caught herself. Much of her father's work involved confidential contracts and sensitive delivery schedules. Claudia had learned not to ask too many questions about it.

"The main pharmaceutical research facility there—you know, Yendor's largest drug development operation," her father said. "They've been working on this experimental treatment for over three years. Today's the day it finally ships out for distribution trials."

"And bring the spectral analyzer on our vacation?" Claudia asked eagerly, changing the subject.

"Wouldn't think of leaving it home," her father said, smiling. "By the way, I calibrated it last week. The sensors are quite sensitive now. Be careful with the settings when you're taking readings."

"I will," Claudia promised. She had accidentally maxed out the sensitivity several times before, getting false positives.

It took Claudia over an hour to sort through the recycling in the garage, separate the materials properly, and haul them to the curb for pickup. By that time, the sun was high overhead, driving off the cool morning air that had made the early hours pleasant.

"Anything else, Mom?" she asked, returning inside and retrieving the spectral analyzer from the equipment closet. She edged toward the back door before her mother had much time to think of additional chores.

"I guess not, dear," Dr. Kim said, smiling at her daughter's hasty retreat. "What are you planning to do?"

"Some environmental sampling," Claudia said.

"Where?"

"Probably around the research campus," Claudia said. The more she thought about it, the more she realized it was too late in the day to go all the way to Timberline. That was a two-hour drive, and she'd need her mother to take her. Besides, there were plenty of other locations around Newbridge where interesting environmental data could be collected.

"Are you going alone?" her mother asked.

"I'll probably stop by and see if Wei wants to come," Claudia answered casually. She tried to make it sound like she'd be doing Wei Mason a favor. After all, he was just a friend from school. Claudia didn't think Wei would make the best research partner, but most of her other friends were away at summer programs or traveling with their families.

"He'll enjoy it, I'm sure," her mother said.

"I'll be back in time for dinner."

"That's fine, dear. Have fun."

Wei Mason lived three blocks away in a modest apartment building. Claudia walked over and knocked on his door.

"Oh, hey, Claudia," Wei greeted her, appearing at the door. "I was hoping you'd come by."

"Well, I just happened to be heading out," Claudia said. "Thought you might want to help me collect some environmental samples with the spectral analyzer. But maybe you're busy."

That's how to handle it, Claudia thought. Don't seem too eager. Let Wei be eager. Then maybe he'll even offer to bring some snacks.

"I'd love to go," Wei said enthusiastically, "but I'm just finishing up my creative writing assignment for summer enrichment. Come on in."

"I'm kind of in a hurry."

"I'll only be a few minutes." He held the door open. "I'll pack us some snacks too."

"All right," Claudia said, stepping inside.

Wei grabbed his laptop from the kitchen table. "You can read what I've written if you want," he said. "It's about institutional reform in healthcare systems."

"Sounds heavy," Claudia said.

"The assignment was to explore applied ethics through narrative," Wei explained. "I'm arguing that better supply chain management in medical distribution could improve social welfare outcomes. Pretty relevant, actually."

"My dad would agree with that," Claudia said. "He deals with that stuff every day."

"How is your dad?" Wei asked, typing quickly. "Still managing operations?"

"Yeah," Claudia said. "He was talking this morning about some big shipment from that pharmaceutical facility in Lincoln. Apparently it's been in development for years."

"Cool," Wei said, finishing his document and closing his laptop. "Okay, I'm ready. Let me just grab some fruit and crackers."

They walked past the Newbridge Institute campus, where Claudia's mother worked as a senior researcher in environmental health. The Institute was known for its work in bioethics and public health policy. As they headed toward the wooded areas beyond the campus, Claudia periodically activated the spectral analyzer. The device's screen displayed wavelength patterns and chemical signatures, but the readings showed nothing unusual—just normal background levels of common minerals and organic compounds.

After they had hiked and sampled most of the morning, Claudia said, "We might as well head back, Wei. Nothing interesting out here today."

"That's fine with me," Wei agreed, wiping sweat from his forehead. "Pretty hot anyway. Let's eat our snacks and go back."

"All right," Claudia said. "You know, one of these days I'd like to go out to that old industrial site near Timberline and do some sampling. Maybe we'll find something significant there." Then she told Wei about her dream.

Wei smiled. "A dream isn't exactly statistical inference," he said, "but I've heard there are some interesting abandoned facilities out there. I'll go anytime you want, Claudia." He handed her an apple.

It was mid-afternoon by the time they returned to Claudia's house. They worked for a while on a documentary project Wei was developing about environmental justice in former industrial communities. Then Wei said goodbye and headed home.

After putting the spectral analyzer back in the equipment closet, Claudia went into the kitchen.

"What's for dinner, Mom?" she asked.

Dr. Kim turned from the counter. Claudia knew immediately, just from the expression on her mother's face, that something was wrong.

"Dinner?" her mother said distractedly. "It's not quite four o'clock yet, Claudia. Besides, dinner may be delayed today."

"But this morning you said it would be on time," Claudia reminded her, puzzled.

"This morning I didn't know what might happen."

Then Claudia heard the sound of her father's voice coming from the study. There was a strange, strained quality to it. The door to the study was ajar. Claudia walked through the living room and glanced inside. Her father sat rigidly at his desk, speaking urgently into his phone. Claudia caught only fragments of the conversation. Then her father ended the call, looked up, and saw Claudia.

If there had been any doubt in Claudia's mind about something being wrong, it vanished now. Mr. Kim looked years older than he had that morning. Worry was etched deeply in his face. He drummed his fingers nervously on the desk.

"Hello, sweetheart," he said. He didn't even ask whether Claudia had discovered any interesting environmental data that day. Usually, he showed genuine interest in her scientific pursuits.

"Dad," Claudia said anxiously, "what—what's wrong?"

"It shows that much, does it?" her father said wearily.

"What's wrong, Dad?" Claudia pressed. "Can you tell me?"

Mr. Kim leaned back in his chair. "Quite a bit is wrong, Claudia," he said, "and I suppose there's no reason not to tell you. It'll be on the news tonight anyway."

"The news?"

"Claudia, you remember me mentioning this morning about that shipment from the pharmaceutical facility in Lincoln?"

"I remember," Claudia said. "Did it arrive?"

"The truck pulled up to our loading dock right on schedule," her father said. "The driver came inside to complete his paperwork at the security desk. When he returned to unload, the refrigerated case was gone."

"Gone?"

"Stolen, Claudia," her father said slowly. "Someone cut through the truck's rear door while it sat at our dock."

CHAPTER TWO

At the moment, Claudia didn't press for more information about the theft. Her father clearly had enough on his mind. The full story was in the evening news broadcast, which Claudia pulled up on her tablet as soon as the alert came through.

She brought the tablet to her father to watch first. After viewing it, Mr. Kim handed the device back to Claudia and leaned back thoughtfully in his chair.

"They've got the basic facts right," Mr. Kim said, "but I'm afraid this is going to cause considerable trouble."

"It wasn't your fault, was it, Dad?" Claudia said defensively.

"Security at the pharmaceutical facility in Lincoln is top-notch," her father said. "Armed guards, biometric access, the works. They loaded that case under constant surveillance. Every step of the journey was tracked by GPS until the truck reached us. And then..." He trailed off.

"But wasn't it in a secure container?" Claudia asked.

"Of course," her father said. "There were approximately fifty doses of a new experimental treatment in a specialized refrigerated case. The pharmaceutical company spent millions developing their security protocols. They have cameras everywhere, restricted access zones, background checks on all personnel. Their facility is practically a fortress."

"Fifty doses," Claudia said thoughtfully. "That's a lot of medicine to steal, isn't it?"

"Not when it's in a compact refrigerated case," her father replied. "No bigger than a small cooler, actually. The pharmaceutical facility in Lincoln had it specially designed—state-of-the-art temperature monitoring, tamper-evident seals, the whole package."

"Even so, nobody could just walk off with it without being noticed," Claudia said.

"That's what's so frustrating," her father said grimly. "The pharmaceutical company did everything right. Their security is impeccable. The shipment was protected every second it was in their custody. But somewhere between the truck arriving and the driver coming back outside..." He shook his head.

Claudia read the news report carefully. The delivery truck from Lincoln in Yendor, where one of the country's leading pharmaceutical research facilities was located, had arrived at its destination. The driver had left the vehicle and gone inside to check in, completing the standard receiving procedures. It had taken him less than ten minutes.

During that brief window, someone had cut through the truck's rear door lock and taken the refrigerated case containing the experimental medication.

Security camera footage showed two individuals in maintenance uniforms approaching the truck while it sat at the dock, though their faces were obscured by caps and masks. A bolt cutter had been left at the scene—a common type available at any hardware store. There were no fingerprints or other identifying marks on it. The camera angles were insufficient to capture useful identifying details. Vehicles had been coming and going all afternoon—delivery vans, supply trucks, employee cars. Nothing unusual had registered.

"Dad," Claudia asked, looking up from the tablet, "how could anyone carry away something that size without being noticed?"

"Our parking area isn't restricted during business hours," her father said. "Anyone could have been waiting nearby. The pharmaceutical facility has checkpoints and perimeter fencing. We don't. We're just not set up the same way."

"But, Dad," Claudia continued, "how would they know when to make their move?"

"That's what haunts me," her father said. "They had maybe eight minutes. The driver walked in, I verified his credentials, we reviewed the manifest together. He needed to use the restroom. By the time we went back out through the warehouse to the dock, the case was gone."

"I don't understand why anyone would steal experimental medication," Claudia said. "Maybe they thought there was something more valuable in that case."

"That's unlikely, dear," Mr. Kim said. "Believe me, this was no ordinary theft. The pharmaceutical facility kept this shipment under wraps. Very few people knew about it. Someone had information they shouldn't have had."

"What kind of information?" Claudia asked.

"The experimental treatment is a new formulation—highly confidential and extremely valuable. The pharmaceutical company has invested enormous resources into its development. They chose our facility to conduct distribution trials because we're smaller, more representative of the kind of operations that would eventually need to handle these medications."

"Distribution trials?" Claudia said. "That sounds important."

"It is important," her father said. "This relates to design science in healthcare logistics—finding optimal ways to distribute medications that require strict temperature control. The research has implications for improving access to life-saving treatments in underserved areas. The pharmaceutical facility in Lincoln developed the medication; our job was to prove that facilities like ours could safely receive and store it."

"You mean this was about more than just medicine?" Claudia asked.

"It's about public health infrastructure," her father explained. "If we can prove that smaller operations can safely handle sensitive biologics, it could revolutionize how medications reach patients in remote or underserved communities. That's why this is so serious."

"But, Dad," Claudia wondered, "what would thieves do with it?"

"They could attempt to reverse-engineer the formulation," her father explained. "Or they could sell it to competitors. The pharmaceutical industry is cutthroat. Some companies engage in industrial espionage to gain advantages in drug development. There are also black markets for experimental treatments, though that's more dangerous—using unproven medications outside of clinical trials raises serious bioethics concerns."

"What happens to the medication if it's not stored properly?" Claudia asked.

"The case has about twelve hours of battery backup for temperature control. After that, if whoever took it doesn't have proper refrigeration equipment, those medications could degrade. They could become worthless—or worse, dangerous."

"Dinner's ready," Claudia's mother called from the kitchen.

During dinner, Claudia found it hard to focus on her food. The idea of pharmaceutical theft kept occupying her thoughts. By the time dessert was finished, she wanted to talk with someone, but she knew she shouldn't burden her father with more questions. She asked if she could visit Wei for a while.

"Well, you were together most of the day," her mother said, "but I suppose it's all right. Be back in an hour, though."

It was a pleasant evening. Claudia walked quickly down the street to Wei's apartment building.

Wei answered her knock.

"Come on in, Claudia," he said, looking surprised. "Dad and I are just finishing dinner."

"Oh, I thought you'd be done by now," Claudia apologized, following him inside.

"Hello, Claudia," Mr. Mason said, but he seemed less cheerful than usual.

"Good evening, Mr. Mason," Claudia said. "I hope I'm not interrupting."

"You're never an interruption, Claudia," Mr. Mason assured her. "I was going to call your mother later about that news report."

"Oh, you saw it?" Claudia said.

"Hard to miss it," Wei said. "It's all over social media. Something about a theft at a pharmaceutical facility?"

"That's not exactly—" Claudia started, then paused. "It's complicated."

"I imagine your father is quite concerned," Wei's father said.

"Yes, very," Claudia confirmed. "The shipment was supposed to be under his supervision once it arrived."

"The news made it sound like the pharmaceutical company in Lincoln was breached," Wei said. "They were showing footage of their facility, talking about their security measures."

"That's misleading," Claudia said carefully. "The pharmaceutical facility wasn't where it happened. The truck had already left Lincoln by then. It was..."

She hesitated, remembering her father's exhaustion, his guilt over what had occurred on his watch.

"The pharmaceutical facility has incredible security," Claudia continued. "The news kept showing their guards, their checkpoints, their cameras. But by the time the truck reached its destination, it was in a completely different environment. The driver went inside to complete paperwork. He was only gone a few minutes. But that was enough time for someone to cut through the truck's door and take the case."

"Where was the truck when this happened?" Wei asked.

"Parked at a loading dock," Claudia said. "The driver had just arrived and went inside to check in. When he came back out with my dad, the case was gone."

"That's deeply troubling," Mr. Mason said. He glanced at the clock. "Speaking of which, I need to make some calls. We've been having our own problems at the media production studio today."

"Problems?" Claudia asked.

"Nothing as serious as your father's situation," Mr. Mason said, "but we had some equipment go missing from the studio. Probably just misplaced, but with everything going on, it makes you wonder."

"What kind of equipment?" Wei asked his father.

"Some recording devices and hard drives," Mr. Mason said. "We use them for documentary work—the kind of artistic expression that preserves collective memory of communities. Losing that footage would be devastating for the people whose stories we're documenting."

"I hope you find it," Claudia said.

"So do I," Mr. Mason replied. "Well, I'd better get to those calls. Nice seeing you, Claudia."

"You too, Mr. Mason."

After Wei's father left the room, Wei turned to Claudia. "This is all pretty scary," he said. "The news keeps talking about the pharmaceutical facility's security failures, but from what you're saying, that's not where the theft actually occurred."

"The pharmaceutical facility didn't have any failures," Claudia said. "Their security is apparently excellent. They loaded the case under constant surveillance and tracked it the entire journey. The problem was what happened after the truck reached its destination."

"So the news has it wrong?" Wei asked.

"The news is focused on the pharmaceutical company because that's where the medication came from," Claudia said. "They developed it, they manufactured it, they have all the fancy security footage. But the truck had already completed its trip from Lincoln. It was sitting at the receiving dock when the theft occurred."

"Your dad's receiving dock," Wei said quietly.

Claudia nodded. "The driver walked inside to complete his paperwork with my dad. Standard procedure. Takes less than ten minutes. But that was enough time for someone to cut through the truck's door and disappear with the case."

"Do you think the police will catch whoever did it?" Wei asked.

"I don't know," Claudia said. "My dad seemed pretty worried about it. He said the thieves were professionals—they knew what they were doing. They had maybe eight minutes, and they used every second."

"Maybe they'll make a mistake," Wei suggested. "Criminals usually do, right?"

"I hope so," Claudia said. "For everyone's sake."

She glanced at Wei's wall clock. "I should probably head home. My mom said to be back in an hour."

"Okay," Wei said. "Thanks for explaining what really happened. The news made it sound like the pharmaceutical facility was breached."

"That's what my dad is worried about," Claudia said. "If people think this happened at the pharmaceutical facility in Lincoln, they might not look at what actually went wrong. The truck was secure for the whole journey. It was only after it arrived and sat unattended for those few minutes that anyone had the opportunity to take anything."

"Just don't mention my dad specifically," Claudia added. "He's got enough problems right now."

"I won't," Wei promised. "See you tomorrow?"

"Sure," Claudia said. "Maybe we can do some more environmental sampling. Or work on your documentary project."

"Sounds good," Wei said.

As Claudia walked home in the evening twilight, she couldn't stop thinking about the stolen medication. Who would do such a thing? And why? The answers eluded her, but she knew one thing for certain: her father was facing the biggest challenge of his career, and there was nothing she could do to help him except be supportive and hope that somehow, everything would work out all right.

When she arrived home, both her parents were in the study, talking quietly. They looked up as she entered.

"Hi, sweetheart," her mother said. "How was your visit with Wei?"

"Good," Claudia said. "We talked about what happened."

"I figured you would," her father said with a tired smile. "I hope I didn't ruin your summer with all this worry."

"You didn't ruin anything, Dad," Claudia said firmly. "This isn't your fault. The pharmaceutical facility should have arranged for better security during the handoff."

Her father shook his head slowly. "The pharmaceutical facility did their part, Claudia. They got the shipment to us safely. What happened after the truck pulled up to our dock—that's on us. That's on me."

"But you can't control everything," Claudia protested. "Those thieves would have found a way no matter what you did."

Her father smiled more genuinely this time. "You know what? You might be right about that. Thank you, Claudia. I needed to hear that."

"We all need to support each other right now," Dr. Kim said, putting her arm around Claudia's shoulders. "Whatever happens, we'll get through it together."

"Absolutely," Claudia agreed, feeling a surge of determination. Her family was strong. They would weather this crisis, just as they had weathered others. And somehow, she hoped, the stolen medication would be recovered and the research program would continue. Too many people were counting on it for the outcome to be anything less.
